claims.text: The patient's pre-term birth at 32 weeks' gestation is a recognized risk factor for early-onset neonatal infection, as defined by the guideline's list of risk factors.
The patient's maternal GBS status is currently unknown; maternal GBS colonisation, bacteriuria, or infection in the current pregnancy is a documented risk factor for early-onset neonatal infection.
The patient's red flags are not fully documented; the guideline identifies specific red flag risk factors for early-onset neonatal infection that should be assessed.

The patient's culture status is unknown; the guideline recommends establishing hospital systems to provide blood culture results 36 hours after starting antibiotics to allow timely stopping of treatment.

The patient's CRP has decreased from 21 at 12 hours to 9 at 24 hours and 6 at 36 hours; the guideline does not specify CRP monitoring intervals, so this trend is an observed patient measurement without direct guideline support for interpretation.

The patient's culture status is unknown; the guideline recommends establishing hospital systems to provide blood culture results 36 hours after starting antibiotics to allow timely stopping of treatment and discharge from hospital.

packet.evaluation_question: Explain appropriate initial diagnostic investigations for suspected early-onset sepsis and the limitations of laboratory tests. Gestation 32 weeks; age 36 hours; setting hospital birth.

evidence.text: For guidance on managing prelabour rupture of membranes at term, see NICE's guideline on intrapartum care. [2021] Box 1: Risk factors for early-onset neonatal infection, including 'red flags' Red flag risk factor: • suspected or confirmed infection in another baby in the case of a multiple pregnancy Other risk factors: • invasive group B streptococcal infection in a previous baby or maternal group B streptococcal colonisation, bacteriuria or infection in the current pregnancy • pre-term birth following spontaneous labour before 37 weeks' gestation • confirmed rupture of membranes for more than 18 hours before a pre-term birth • confirmed rupture of membranes for more than 24 hours before a term birth [2026] • suspected or confirmed maternal sepsis in the intrapartum or early postpartum period [2021, amended 2026] • suspected or confirmed chorioamnionitis [2021, amended 2026]

Risk factors and clinical indicators: early- onset neonatal infection 1.9 Identification and assessment before birth 1.9.1 For women, trans men and non-binary people in labour, identify and assess any risk factors for early-onset neonatal infection (see box 1 on risks factors for early- onset neonatal infection). Throughout labour, monitor for any new risk factors. [2021] 1.9.2 For guidance on managing prelabour rupture of membranes at term, see NICE's guideline on intrapartum care. [2021] Box 1: Risk factors for early-onset neonatal infection, including 'red flags' Red flag risk factor: • suspected or confirmed infection in another baby in the case of a multiple pregnancy Other risk factors: • invasive group B streptococcal infection in a previous baby or maternal group B streptococcal colonisation, bacteriuria or infection in the current pregnancy • pre-term birth following spontaneous labour before 37 weeks' gestation • confirmed rupture of membranes for more than 18 hours before a pre-term birth • confirmed rupture of membranes for more than 24 hours before a term birth [2026] • suspected or confirmed maternal sepsis in the intrapartum or early postpartum period [2021, amended 2026] • suspected or confirmed chorioamnionitis [2021, amended 2026]

Consider establishing hospital systems to provide blood culture results 36 hours after starting antibiotics for early-onset neonatal infection, to allow timely stopping of treatment and discharge from hospital. [2012]

Offer an immediate birth (by induction of labour or caesarean birth) to women, trans men and non-binary people who are between 34 and 37 weeks' gestation who: • have prolonged prelabour rupture of membranes and • have group B streptococcal colonisation, bacteriuria or infection at any time in their current pregnancy. [2021]
